rows.speaker: Fahr-i Râzî
rows.claim: Rāzī argues that the Elephant episode is a crucial proof against skeptics: ordinary natural laws cannot explain birds selectively destroying one army, and its public, near-contemporary transmission cannot be dismissed as weak.
rows.anchor: Fahr-i Râzî der ki: “Bu fil vak‘ası mülhidlere karşı cidden pek mühim bir vak‘adır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı endorses Rāzī: hostile Meccans had every opportunity to challenge the account, yet none denied it, so its occurrence as described is certain and widely transmitted.
rows.anchor: yerindedir. Sûrenin Mekkî olduğu ve Mekke’de iken düşmanların çokluğu

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Had the account contained a refutable weakness, Muhammad’s enemies and poets would have seized the chance to expose him; the author links this counterfactual to the warning in al-Ḥāqqah.
rows.anchor: o vakit Sûre-i Hâkka’da geçtiği üzere

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many contemporaries even composed poems affirming the episode, and its truth was as undeniable to people as the existence of the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: evvel ü âhir birçokları o kıssanın doğruluğu hakkında şiirler söylemişlerdir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode is an extraordinary divine act that should yield lessons, rather than be reduced to familiar natural laws to avoid its miraculous character.
rows.anchor: tabiatlar üzerinde hâkim ve mutasarrıf olan Hak teâlâ’nın fevkalâde olan bir fi‘l-i rabbânîsi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated events seem ordinary and enter scientific laws, while rare events may exceed current models without contradicting reason; recorded anomalies can later inform inquiry.
rows.anchor: Tekerrür etmedikçe de acîb, garîb, şaz, münferid bir vak‘a olarak görünür

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Science and serious history should record unusual observations faithfully, assess narrators’ reliability, and avoid rejecting a repeatedly transmitted event merely because no parallel is seen.
rows.anchor: mislini görmüyoruz diye inkâra veya tevile kalkışmak ne fen, ne de tarih

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sudden hail of stones from birds could injure and kill an army like crushed grain; it is unusual but possible and contains no rational contradiction, while displaying divine power.
rows.anchor: Bir sahrada bir ordu üzerine ansızın bir kuş akını ve onlarla semâdan dolu gibi taş yağdırılması

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People cannot know what prompted the birds, but the episode makes divine will visible, as every event ordinarily called natural should also do.
rows.anchor: Ancak biz o kuşların ne gibi hislerle uçtuklarını ve nasıl bir his ile

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God addresses the Prophet as if he saw the event because he grew up amid its many witnesses and knew its details through public transmission reaching near eyewitness knowledge.
rows.anchor: şuhûd ve tevâtürü ile bilgi, rü’yet ile müşahede bilgisine müntehî olduğu için

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The event’s shared core as stated in the Qur’an is mutawātir; conflicting details are not all sound and must be weighed by their chains and fit with the verses.
rows.anchor: Tafsîlâtına müte‘allik olan rivâyâta gelince onların buna muvâfık olan kadr-i müşterekleri

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı extends the discussion because reports of smallpox and measles were being used to naturalize the miracle and bend the clear meanings of the birds and stones toward a microbial explanation.
rows.anchor: âyet sarih olan mânasından çıkarılarak kuşların ve taşların mânası buraya doğru eğilmek istenildiği cihetle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The historical account begins with Dhu Nuwās, who embraced Judaism and persecuted the monotheist Christians of Najrān in the trench massacre; a survivor escaped to seek aid.
rows.anchor: Zûnüvâs Yahudîliği iltizam etmiş ve o vakit Necran’dan hâlis tevhid esası üzere intişar etmekte bulunan muvahhid Îsevî mü’minleri çevirmek için uhdûd vak‘asını ihdas ederek katliam yapmıştı.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The survivor appealed to the Roman emperor, who asked the nearby Christian Abyssinian king for help; Najāshī sent a large force under Aryāṭ, with Abraha among its officers.
rows.anchor: Habeş’ten yetmiş bin kişilik bir ordu tertip edip

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the Yemenis were defeated and Dhu Nuwās drowned, Aryāṭ ruled Yemen; Abraha then killed Aryāṭ by a ruse and took power, later appeasing Najāshī with his shaved head and a bag of Yemeni soil.
rows.anchor: Ebrehe Eryat’ı mübarezeye davet edip kölesi Atûde’yi arkasında saklayarak bir desîse ile Eryat’ı öldürüp yerine geçmişti.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraha built the unprecedented Kullays church in San‘ā and announced that he would redirect Arab pilgrimage there, provoking the Kaaba expedition.
rows.anchor: Sonra bu Ebrehe San‘â’da Kulleys yapmış

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says a man from the Nasa’ calendar-keeping tribe defiled the church’s qibla; another says a caravan fire spread to it, and Abraha vowed to destroy the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: bir rivayette de bir Arap kafilesi kilisenin civarında bir ateş yakmışlarmış.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accounts vary on the invading force’s size and number of elephants: the famous version gives sixty thousand soldiers, Mahmud, and eight, twelve, or more other war elephants.
rows.anchor: denildiğine göre altmış bin kişilik bir ordu, beraberlerinde Necâşî’nin fili olan ve “Mahmud” denilen büyük bir fil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab leaders first resisted: Dhu Nufr was defeated and captured but spared, and Nufayl ibn Habib’s Khath‘am forces were defeated before Nufayl offered to guide Abraha.
rows.anchor: Ey melik, beni öldürme! Bu Arap arzında ben sana

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Ṭā’if, Thaqīf leaders said the targeted sanctuary was the Meccan Kaaba rather than their own al-Lāt shrine, and supplied a guide; Abū Righāl died en route and Arabs stoned his grave.
rows.anchor: bizde sana muhalefet edecek yok ve senin kasdettiğin Beyt bizim beytimiz değil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraha’s cavalry seized the people’s property, including two hundred camels belonging to the Prophet’s grandfather ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; local tribes considered fighting but judged themselves too weak.
rows.anchor: bu arada cedd-i Nebî Hazret-i Abdülmuttalib’in de iki yüz kadar devesini sürüp götürmüşler.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraha sent Hunāṭa to summon Mecca’s chief and explain that the expedition sought to demolish the sanctuary, not fight the people unless they resisted.
rows.anchor: Ben size harb etmek için gelmedim, ancak şu beyti yıkmak için geldim.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib said his people could not fight the army, and that the Kaaba belonged to God, who would protect it if He wished.
rows.anchor: vallahi biz ona harb etmek fikrinde değiliz, ona tâkatimiz yok

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu Nufr arranged for the elephant keeper Unays to introduce ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; Abraha received him with honor, but was surprised he asked only for his camels.
rows.anchor: Abdülmuttalib gayet iri ve pek yakışıklı, insanlar güzeli idi. Ebrehe onu görünce iclâl ile tâzim ve ikram etti

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Abraha asked why he did not plead for the Kaaba, ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib answered that he owned the camels while the House had a Lord who would protect it.
rows.anchor: ben o develerin sâhibiyim, o Beyt’in ise bir Rabbi vardır. Onu men‘edecek odur

rows.speaker: İbn İshak
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq says some learned people claimed two other tribal chiefs offered Abraha a third of Tihāma’s wealth to turn back, but he himself was unsure whether this occurred.
rows.anchor: İbn İshak demiştir ki: Bazı ehl-i ilmin zu‘muna göre Ebrehe Hunâta’yı gönderdiği zaman

rows.speaker: İbn Hişam
rows.claim: Ibn Hisham judges the account given up to this point to be authentic.
rows.anchor: İbn Hişam der ki: “Bunun bu kadarı sahih olanıdır.

rows.speaker: Abdülmuttalib
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib’s poem asks God to protect His sanctuary and its sacred precinct even as a servant guards his own property from the enemy.
rows.anchor: لاَهُمّ إنَّ الْعَبْدَ يَمْنَعُ رَحْلَهُ فَامْنَعْ حِلَاَلَ ك

rows.speaker: İkrime b. Amr b. Hâşim
rows.claim: Ikrima’s poem asks God to punish al-Aswad ibn Maqsud for taking the herd and restrain the enemy who seized it.
rows.anchor: İkrime b. Amr b. Hâşim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the army moved toward Mecca, Mahmud knelt and would not rise despite beating, pulling, or wine; it ran when turned toward Yemen, and Nufayl had earlier made it kneel.
rows.anchor: Nüfeyl b. Habib varıp[^94] filin yanına yanaşmış

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Wādī Muḥassir, God sent birds from the sea like swallows and balsam birds; each carried three chickpea- or lentil-sized stones, which killed those they struck, though not everyone was hit.
rows.anchor: Allah teâlâ denizden üzerlerine أَمْثَال الخَطَاطِيفِ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scattered army fled and kept asking for Nufayl to show the road to Yemen; Nufayl answered that there was nowhere to escape from God’s pursuer.
rows.anchor: geldikleri yolu tutmak istiyorlar, Yemen yolunu göstersin diye hep Nüfeyl’i soruşturuyorlardı

rows.speaker: Nüfeyl b. Habîb
rows.claim: Nufayl’s ode says he thanked God after seeing the birds and fearing stones, while all the Abyssinians were asking for him as if he owed them a debt.
rows.anchor: O vakit Nüfeyl onların başlarına gelen bu hâli görünce şöyle demişti

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The soldiers fell and died along their route; Abraha was injured, his flesh shed in fingertip-sized pieces with pus and blood, and he reached San‘ā like a fledgling before his heart burst.
rows.anchor: her yolda düşüşüyorlardı. Ve her sığındıkları yerde helâk oluyorlardı, Ebrehe de cesedinden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports describe larger, differently colored birds and stones as large as a human head; the famous account is the one just given, though one person reportedly escaped to Najāshī.
rows.anchor: Yukarıda geçtiği üzere kuşların daha ziyade cesâmeti

rows.speaker: İbn İshak
rows.claim: A single report transmitted by Ibn Isḥāq from Ya‘qūb ibn ʿUtba, on an unnamed informant’s authority, says measles, smallpox, and certain bitter plants first appeared in Arabia that year.
rows.anchor: tek bir haber olarak demiştir ki: “Bana Ya‘kūb b. Utbe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı calls the Ya‘qūb report weak because it is one account through an unknown informant; it does not say the army died of disease, so those phenomena may have followed the event.
rows.anchor: yalnız Ya‘kūb b. Utbe’den bir tek rivayet olduğu

rows.speaker: İkrime
rows.claim: A report from Ikrima says the birds were green, came from the sea with beasts’ heads, and pelted the army; anyone struck developed smallpox, which had never appeared before.
rows.anchor: İkrime طَيْرًا أَبَابِيلَ kavlinde demiş ki

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Ikrima’s report, the eaten-straw outcome involves both the stones’ external wounds and immediate internal smallpox; stones and disease together make the event doubly extraordinary.
rows.anchor: hem de o taşların tesiriyle aynı zamanda çiçek çıkartıp kırmak, iki garâbetle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other accounts do not say the stone-struck army died of smallpox; only Abraha’s decaying body might suggest a separate illness, perhaps smallpox.
rows.anchor: Diğer rivayetlerde kuşlarla taşlanan askerin çiçekten kırıldığına dair bir söz yoktur.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disease theory rests only on two isolated, weak reports: one anonymous and one ending at Ikrima; although he often reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, that link is unproven here.
rows.anchor: biri mechulde biri de İkrime’de kesilmiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Smallpox and measles first appearing that year is possible, but the plants’ first appearance and an epidemic caused alongside the stoning are highly unusual; some therefore called the report munkar.
rows.anchor: Arabistan’da çiçek ve kızamık hastalıklarının ilk olarak o sene görülmüş ve bir daha görülmemiş olması garib görülmezse de

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentaries omit the disease report, while some mention it briefly while signaling its weakness; readers who accept it must preserve its double wonder and not use it to make the event ordinary.
rows.anchor: tefsirlerin çoğu bunu kāle almamış oldukları hâlde bazıları da ihtimâli nazar-ı dikkate alarak

rows.speaker: Hammer
rows.claim: Hammer suggests the Abyssinian ruler’s campaign may have been halted by an infectious smallpox illness as well as the birds’ stones.
rows.anchor: İşbu fil senesinde Habeş hükümdarı Kâbe üzerine yürürken kuşların askeri üzerine attığı taşlarla, ihtimal ki bir çiçek illet-i sâriyesiyle tevakkufa mecbur olmuştur.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı says Hammer’s word ‘halted’ subtly minimizes the defeat, though he appreciates that Hammer calls smallpox only a possibility and still mentions the stones.
rows.anchor: tevakkufa mecbur olmuştur” deyip geçmesi, vak‘anın ehemmiyetini nazardan ıskāt yolunda kurnaz bir kalem oyunu olmuştur.

rows.speaker: Abduh
rows.claim: Abduh says the surah teaches God’s overwhelming power: an elephant-backed people sought to overcome His servants, but their numbers and preparations did not help when God destroyed their plot.
rows.anchor: Allah sübhânehu Peygamberine ve onun risaletinin bâliğ olacağı kimselere kudretinin büyüklüğünü

rows.speaker: Abduh
rows.claim: Abduh says this moral lesson could suffice without further detail, as he had done with the People of the Trench.
rows.anchor: ashâb-ı uhdûdda bu kadarla iktifâ etmiştik

rows.speaker: Abduh
rows.claim: Abduh allows detail because the Elephant event was famous and mutawātir and the year became a dating epoch; Elmalılı agrees this historical claim is true.
rows.anchor: fil vak‘ası bu âyetlerde vârid olduğu gibi haddizâtında mâruf ve rivayeti mütevâtirdir

rows.speaker: Abduh
rows.claim: Abduh’s summary of the mutawātir account is that an Abyssinian commander came with a huge army and elephants to demolish the Kaaba, defeated everyone on the way, and sent a message to Mecca before its people fled.
rows.anchor: Abduh verdiği tafsilde mütevâtirle kalmamış, tevâtüre karşı zayıf ve indî mütalaa ile ihticâca kalkışmıştır, mütevâtir olan kısmı şöyle hulâsa ediyor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı rejects the idea that only mutawātir reports may be detailed: sound solitary reports can suffice as evidence, and even weak non-fabricated reports may be included for historical knowledge and admonition.
rows.anchor: sıhhati tam ve sâbit olmasa bile yalan ve uydurma, mevzû‘olduğu sâbit olmayan zayıf rivayetler dahi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı calls Abduh’s summary incomplete for omitting Abraha and ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib’s names, but accepts its outline as correct and mutawātir.
rows.anchor: Ne Ebrehe’nin ne de Abdülmuttalib Hazretleri’nin isimlerini bile kāle almayan bu ifade eksik olmakla beraber doğrudur ve mütevâtirdir.

rows.speaker: Abduh
rows.claim: Abduh claims smallpox and measles spread in the Abyssinian army on the second day and presents this as mutawātir; Elmalılı says that wording is his own construction, while the transmitted account says birds stoned and destroyed them.
rows.anchor: İkinci gün ise Habeş askeri içinde dâ-i cüderî ve hasbe fâş oluverdi” diyor.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı says Abduh recasts the extraordinary bird-and-stone event as ordinary, as though no power could raise birds carrying stones to strike an army from the sky.
rows.anchor: o büyük işi âdî gibi göstermeyi bir fevkalâdelik saymıştır.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abduh derives the second-day epidemic claim by combining two weak reports and omitting their context; the reports neither are mutawātir nor corroborate each other as he implies.
rows.anchor: Abduh “ikinci günü Habeş ordusunda çiçek ve kızamık illeti fâş oldu” lâkırdısını bu iki sözden istidlâl

rows.speaker: İkrime
rows.claim: Ikrima’s report says that anyone struck by a stone immediately developed smallpox; it does not merely report an army-wide epidemic.
rows.anchor: Gördük ki İkrime kuşları ve attıkları taşları söylemekle beraber, o taşlar kime isabet ettiyse cüderî çıkarttığını

rows.speaker: Ya‘kūb b. Utbe
rows.claim: Ya‘qūb’s anonymous report says measles, smallpox, and certain plants first appeared in Arabia during the Elephant year, which may refer to later effects rather than the battle itself.
rows.anchor: arz-ı Arabda cüderî ve hasbenin ilk görüldüğü o sene ve mirâr-i şecer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı notes that ḥasba can also mean gravel, and rhetorically asks whether that ambiguity prompted Abduh to replace Ikrima’s stones with measles.
rows.anchor: Yoksa “hasbe” kelimesinin kızamıktan başka çakıl mânasına dahi gelmesinden de bir mâna çıkarılmak mı istenildi?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reports do not say that the army’s flesh fell away; they say soldiers fell as they fled, while Abraha alone suffered flesh shedding in fingertip-sized pieces.
rows.anchor: rivayetlerde askerin etlerinin dağılıp düşmesi yoktur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraha’s severe bodily decay could have been smallpox, syphilis, or another unprecedented illness; Elmalılı leaves the specific disease uncertain.
rows.anchor: Bunun ise gayet şedid bir cüderî olması mümkin olduğu gibi bir frengi veya misli görülmedik bir illet olması da mümkindir.

rows.speaker: Abduh
rows.claim: Abduh says the reports agree on his account and that sound belief may rest on it; Elmalılı rejects this as a false attribution because Abduh inserted his own disease theory and then reinterpreted the birds.
rows.anchor: Hâlbuki tevâtürü naklederken kendi vaz‘ını dess ü tedlis ile dahi kalmayıp da هذَا مَا اتـَّفَقَتْ عَلَيْهِ الرِّوَايَاتُ
